name: Tràng An
localName: Quần thể danh thắng Tràng An
summary: Limestone towers, caves and rivers where boats glide through flooded valleys. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for both its nature and its history.

hero.alt: Boats on the river at Tràng An

eras.label: c. 30,000 years ago
eras.title: Hunters in the caves
eras.text: Archaeologists have found traces of people living in the caves of Tràng An over tens of thousands of years. They adapted as the sea rose and fell, sometimes turning the valleys into islands.

eras.title: The capital of Hoa Lư
eras.text: Đinh Bộ Lĩnh chose this maze of mountains for his capital, Hoa Lư, because the limestone formed natural walls. The temples of the Đinh and Lê kings still stand there.

image.file: Dinh Bo Linh Shrine, Hoa Lư, Ninh Bình, Vietnam, 20240203 1458 5685.jpg
image.alt: The temple of King Đinh Bộ Lĩnh at Hoa Lư

eras.title: The court moves away
eras.text: In 1010 Emperor Lý Thái Tổ moved the capital to Thăng Long, today's Hà Nội. Hoa Lư became a quiet place of temples and memories.

image.file: Festival of Dinh and Le kings at Hoa Lu.JPG
image.alt: The festival of the Đinh and Lê kings at Hoa Lư

eras.title: World Heritage
eras.text: UNESCO listed the Tràng An Landscape Complex as a mixed World Heritage Site, for its beauty, its geology and its record of human life.

image.file: Vietnam, Ninh Binh, Limestone mountains, panoramic view from above.jpg

eras.label: Today
eras.title: Through the caves
eras.text: Rowing boats carry visitors along the rivers and through low caves that pass right under the mountains, past temples on the banks.

image.alt: A rowing boat at Tam Cốc

story.title: The buffalo boy who became king

image.file: Dinh Bo Linh Shrine, Hoa Lư, Ninh Bình, Vietnam, 20240203 1458 5685.jpg
image.alt: The temple of Đinh Bộ Lĩnh

story.narration: Đinh Bộ Lĩnh grew up poor, herding buffalo. The story goes that he led the other village boys in mock battles, using reeds as flags, and the children carried him like a king. As a young man in the 960s, when twelve warlords were fighting over the land, he defeated them one by one and united the country. In 968 he declared himself emperor of Đại Cồ Việt, with his capital at Hoa Lư, close to the hills where he had played as a child.

story.title: Rowing with their feet

image.alt: Boats in the rice fields at Tam Cốc

story.narration: At Tam Cốc and Tràng An, many of the boats are rowed by women from the local villages. Some row with their feet, leaning back and pushing the oars with their legs, which lets them rest their arms on the long trips. The boats pass through caves so low that passengers have to duck, and through valleys where the only sounds are the oars and the birds. In early June the rice fields along the river turn gold.

story.title: A heritage of nature and people
story.narration: Tràng An is one of only a few sites in Asia listed by UNESCO for both nature and culture. Its limestone towers were shaped over millions of years. Inside its caves, archaeologists have found tools, shells and animal bones left by people who lived here as the sea level rose after the last Ice Age. Later, the same landscape sheltered Vietnam's first imperial capital. Few places show so clearly how people and landscape shaped each other.

guide.price: Ticket includes a seat on a rowing boat, shared by up to four people. The trip takes about 2–3 hours.

hours.notes: Approximate. Last boats leave in mid-afternoon.

do: Wear a hat and sunscreen. There is no shade on the boats.
Keep your hands inside the boat in the caves.
Visit early to avoid the midday crowds.
Combine Tràng An with the ancient capital of Hoa Lư.
dont: Rush the rowers. The route is slow by design.

tips.title: Local food
tips.text: Ninh Bình is famous for goat meat (dê núi) and crispy burnt rice (cơm cháy); Nam Định for its phở.

tips.title: Getting there
tips.text: About 2 hours from Hà Nội by car or train to Ninh Bình city, then 15 minutes by taxi.

tips.title: Nearby
tips.text: Bái Đính Pagoda, Tam Cốc, the Múa cave viewpoint, and Phát Diệm Cathedral.
